catalogsHero.title: Catalogs
catalogsHero.subtitle: Track your imaging progress through classic observing programs.

messier.label: Messier
messier.tagline: 110 bright showpieces logged by a comet hunter who kept mistaking them for comets.
messier.blurb: Messier logged these 110 fuzzy patches while hunting comets, so he would stop mistaking them for new ones. Every entry is bright enough for a small telescope, which makes this the list most imagers finish first.

caldwell.label: Caldwell
caldwell.tagline: 109 showpieces Messier left out, ordered by declination and reaching deep south.
caldwell.blurb: Patrick Moore picked 109 bright showpieces that Messier left out, ordered by declination and reaching deep into the southern sky. Expect targets the Messier list misses, including the Veil, the Helix, and the Double Cluster.

herschel400.label: Herschel 400
herschel400.tagline: 400 fainter objects from William Herschel's own sweeps. The natural step after Messier.
herschel400.blurb: 400 objects drawn from William Herschel's own sweeps of the sky, chosen as the natural challenge after Messier. Fainter, smaller, and mostly galaxies, so it rewards long integration and dark skies.

sharpless.label: Sharpless
sharpless.tagline: 313 clouds of glowing hydrogen, the emission nebulae behind many of the sky's familiar names.
sharpless.blurb: Stewart Sharpless catalogued 313 HII regions from the National Geographic sky survey plates. These are the hydrogen-alpha clouds narrowband imagers chase: large, faint, and full of structure. Some carry familiar names like the Cave, the Wizard, and the Pacman, but plenty are unnamed fields waiting for a long exposure.

unknown.label: Broadband LRGB
unknown.rationale: There is no filter guidance for this object type, so broadband LRGB is the safe choice.

no-filter.label: No filter
no-filter.rationale: The light here is broad across the spectrum, so a filter would only cost you signal.

no-filter-lrgb.label: No filter, broadband LRGB
no-filter-lrgb.rationale: Broadband LRGB gives the truest color for this object type, and a narrowband filter would reject most of its light.

lrgb.label: Broadband LRGB
lrgb.rationale: Standard LRGB: luminance for detail, RGB for color. Narrowband adds little for this object type.

luminance.label: Luminance or clear filter
luminance.rationale: Start with luminance for detail, then add Ha or OIII only if your skies are heavily light polluted or you want more contrast.

ha-dual.label: Ha or dual narrowband
ha-dual.rationale: Ha brings out the emission detail, and a dual-pass filter such as L-Extreme or Duo-Band also cuts light pollution on a one-shot-color rig.

ha-oiii.label: Ha and OIII
ha-oiii.rationale: Both Ha and OIII carry real signal in this object, so shooting the pair brings out the full two-color structure.

oiii-ha.label: OIII first, then Ha
oiii-ha.rationale: OIII is the dominant line here, and Ha fills in the outer envelope and filaments.

sho.label: SHO (Hubble palette)
sho.rationale: SII, Ha and OIII each show different structure in this object, and the Hubble palette makes the most of all three.
